newsitem.title: UK: Iraq oil sales look tricky without price cut-trade.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil sales look tricky without price cut-trade.

text.p: Iraq will struggle to find customers for the large volumes of crude it is expected to tout on world markets next month without a significant cut in prices, oil traders said on Monday.
Iraqi flows could top 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in August and early September after delays in resuming exports in the third three-month term of the United Nations oil-for-food agreement.

Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) must more than double export rates from the first six-month period if it is to reach its $1-billion revenue target for the current 90-day period which began on June 7.
The U.N. last week said only five percent of sales could be carried over into the next quarter.
"I think it's going to be difficult placing that sort of volume," said the head of trading at a major European oil company.
The new price formula which is still to be finalised will be the key, traders said.

"Anything can be sold if the price is right...and the feeling is that if they want to sell they'll sell it, but only at the expense of moving the market right down," said one regular buyer of Iraqi crude in the first term of sales.
Traders said that sales to Far East markets are likely to be the most difficult because of the long nomination periods for loadings that Asian buyers require.

"A particular problem with any increased sales out of Mina al Bakr to eastern markets because Japanese companies have already booked what they want for August and are looking at September requirements," said one.

Traders said that SOMO may try to get round this by diverting cargoes of Basrah Light, which loads at the Mideast Gulf port of Mina al Bakr, to the U.S. Gulf refining belt by making aggressive cuts in price differentials for U.S. buyers.
Sales into the Mediterranean sour crude market should be less problematic with Iraq's Kirkuk blend, which is piped to the Turkish port of Ceyhan, directly displacing Russian Urals.
"If priced aggressively enough it can displace Urals...it's no real problem for us to switch," said one Mediterranean refiner.
But most traders said they would wait until the new price formula was published before signing contracts.

Iraqi oil minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said last month that the pricing mechanism for Iraqi crude which ties Kirkuk and Basrah Light to regional benchmarks in Europe, Asia, the United States and South Africa will remain the same, but differentials could change.
Traders said they expected SOMO to ask the U.N. for much deeper discounts than in the first six months of sales.
"SOMO doesn't really care how low the price is, the weaker the price, the more market share it can get...but it doesn't want to deplete reserves unnecessarily," said a European buyer of Iraqi crude.
Iraq on Monday cleared the way for discussion of the new pricing formula when it submitted a new aid distribution plans to U.N. officials in New York.
